title: Topical tacrolimus for atopic dermatitis: inhibits T-lymphocyte signaling
vignette: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the clinic due to an itchy rash on her face. The patient's mother says the rash began approximately 3 weeks ago as dry skin on both of her cheeks. Over the past few days, it has progressed with areas of weeping and increased redness, and the patient has had to wear mittens to limit irritation from constant scratching. The patient has a history of similar rashes involving the flexural areas of her elbows and knees that resolved following treatment with topical corticosteroids. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination shows erythema of the bilateral cheeks and chin with crusting and oozing. The patient is prescribed a course of topical tacrolimus. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this drug?

clues.note: A pruritic facial rash in a child, with a relapsing course, fits atopic dermatitis (eczema).

clues.text: flexural areas of her elbows and knees that resolved following treatment with topical corticosteroids
clues.note: Recurrent flexural eczema responsive to topical steroids is classic atopic dermatitis. Prior steroid response sets up why a steroid-sparing agent (calcineurin inhibitor) is now used on the face.

clues.text: erythema of the bilateral cheeks and chin with crusting and oozing
clues.note: Facial involvement with weeping/crusting is typical of childhood atopic dermatitis; the face is a thin-skin site where chronic steroids risk atrophy - hence tacrolimus.
Tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor used as second-line, steroid-sparing therapy for atopic dermatitis (especially face/skin folds). It blocks calcineurin, preventing T-cell activation.

whatMatters: This is atopic dermatitis, and tacrolimus is a topical CALCINEURIN INHIBITOR used as steroid-sparing therapy (good for face/skin folds where steroids cause atrophy). Tacrolimus binds FKBP and inhibits calcineurin, blocking NFAT-driven transcription of IL-2 and thereby INHIBITING T-LYMPHOCYTE SIGNALING/activation. Answer B.
strategy: Identify the drug class from the name: tacrolimus/pimecrolimus/cyclosporine = calcineurin inhibitors -> block IL-2 transcription -> inhibit T-cell activation. That's answer B. Reject mechanisms of other allergy drugs: mast-cell stabilizers (cromolyn - histamine release), anti-IgE (omalizumab - IgE binding to mast cells), anti-IL-4R (dupilumab), and anti-CD20 (rituximab - B-cell depletion).

options.text: Prevention of IgE binding to mast cells
Selective blockade of the IL-4 receptor

eliminations.label: Inhibition of histamine granule release - cromolyn
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: mast-cell stabilizers (cromolyn) prevent mast-cell degranulation/histamine release. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's not how tacrolimus works; tacrolimus inhibits T-cell activation via calcineurin. ✅ Correct if: cromolyn for allergic rhinitis/mastocytosis.

eliminations.label: Prevention of IgE binding to mast cells - omalizumab
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: omalizumab is an anti-IgE antibody that prevents IgE from binding mast cells/basophils. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor, not an anti-IgE agent. ✅ Correct if: omalizumab for severe persistent asthma/urticaria.

eliminations.label: Selective blockade of the IL-4 receptor - dupilumab
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: dupilumab blocks IL-4 receptor signaling (Th2/IgE pathway) in refractory atopic dermatitis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it's a different biologic mechanism than calcineurin inhibition. ✅ Correct if: dupilumab for moderate-severe atopic dermatitis/asthma.

eliminations.label: Stimulation of B-lymphocyte apoptosis - rituximab
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody that depletes B cells (complement/cell-mediated cytotoxicity). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: tacrolimus targets T cells via calcineurin, not B cells. ✅ Correct if: rituximab for CLL or rheumatoid arthritis.

reasoning: Relapsing pruritic flexural/facial eczema in a child = atopic dermatitis
Tacrolimus is a topical calcineurin inhibitor (steroid-sparing; good for thin-skin sites)
It binds FKBP and inhibits calcineurin, blocking NFAT-driven IL-2 transcription
mechanism: Atopic dermatitis is an inflammatory skin disorder of infancy/childhood driven by epidermal barrier dysfunction (e.g., filaggrin mutations) and a dysregulated, Th2-skewed immune response with increased IgE and mast cell/eosinophil activity. First-line therapy is topical corticosteroids, but on thin-skin areas (face, neck, skin folds) chronic steroids cause atrophy, so calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are used as second-line, steroid-sparing agents. Tacrolimus binds the intracellular immunophilin FKBP; the complex inhibits calcineurin, a phosphatase that normally dephosphorylates NFAT to allow transcription of interleukin-2 (IL-2). By inhibiting calcineurin, tacrolimus blocks IL-2 transcription and thereby T-lymphocyte activation and proliferation, reducing the inflammatory response. The distractors are the mechanisms of cromolyn (mast-cell stabilizer), omalizumab (anti-IgE), dupilumab (anti-IL-4R), and rituximab (anti-CD20 B-cell depletion).

memoryHook: Tacrolimus handcuffs calcineurin, so NFAT never turns on IL-2 - T cells stay quiet. Steroid-free calm for the cheeks.
